overview.title: 📖 Overview: Trumpets, Hallel, and the Temple Orchestra
overview.subtitle: Arakhin 10a–10b
overview.hebrewSource: אֵין פּוֹחֲתִין מֵעֶשְׂרִים וְאַחַת תְּקִיעוֹת בַּמִּקְדָּשׁ, וְלֹא מוֹסִיפִין עַל אַרְבָּעִים וּשְׁמֹנֶה
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf opens a new mishna cataloguing more Temple minimums and maximums: the daily trumpet blasts (twenty-one to forty-eight), the lyres (two to six) and flutes (two to twelve) of the Levitical orchestra, and a dispute over the musicians' own lineage. The Gemara notes the mishna's trumpet count follows the Rabbis' view that tekiah, teruah, and tekiah are each counted separately, against Rabbi Yehuda's view that the three form a single unit. It then explains why the flute plays specifically on the twelve days that overlap with the eighteen days of full Hallel, working through why Sukkot gets Hallel every day but Pesach only the first, why Shabbat and Rosh Chodesh are skipped, why Rosh HaShana and Yom Kippur are somber days without song, and why Chanukah's Hallel for a miracle does not extend to Purim. The daf closes with Temple-craft anecdotes: instruments whose 'improved' gold plating or professional repairs only made their sound worse, restored only once the improvements were undone.

rows: 48 — on the Friday of Sukkot's water-drawing

callout.label: Who played them?
callout.text: Three views on the musicians: Rabbi Meir — slaves of priests; Rabbi Yosei — pure-lineage Israelite families who intermarried with priests; Rabbi Ḥanina ben Antigonus — Levites.

slides.title: 🎺 Rabbis vs. Rabbi Yehuda — How Do You Count a Blast?
slides.subtitle: The same sequence of sounds, two different tallies

lines.speaker: Rabbis
lines.text: A tekiah is one unit, a teruah another, and the closing tekiah a third — hence a daily range of 21 to 48 blasts.

lines.speaker: R' Yehuda
lines.text: No — tekiah, teruah, and tekiah together count as ONE unit, so the range is only 7 to 16.

lines.speaker: Rabbis' proof
lines.text: 'And when congregating the assembly, sound a tekiah, and not a teruah' (Numbers 10:7) — if the three were one unit, that verse would demand only HALF a mitzva!

lines.speaker: R' Yehuda replies
lines.text: That congregating-tekiah is merely a signal to gather, not a mitzva-blast at all. A true mitzva blast always comes as a complete set of three.

slides.title: 🎶 Why Hallel Some Days and Not Others?
slides.subtitle: The flute plays on the twelve days that overlap with full Hallel

nodes.content: ❓ Full Hallel is recited every day of Sukkot but only the FIRST day of Pesach — why?
💡 Sukkot's additional offerings change each day (the bull-count shifts); Pesach's stay identical — so only Pesach's first day, when the Festival pattern begins, gets Hallel

columns.label: Shabbat
columns.content: Its offerings differ too — but it is never called a 'mo'ed' (festival), so no Hallel

columns.label: Rosh Chodesh
columns.content: IS called mo'ed, but carries no labor-prohibition — song requires a day 'sanctified' like a Festival

nodes.content: 🕊️ Rosh HaShana/Yom Kippur meet both conditions, yet still NO Hallel: R' Abbahu — the angels asked why, and God answered, 'can Israel sing while the books of life and death lie open before Me?'

slides.title: 🕎 Chanukah, Purim, and a Miracle Outside the Land
slides.subtitle: Three attempts to explain why Purim gets no Hallel

lines.speaker: Gemara
lines.text: Chanukah has no special offering and no labor-prohibition, yet we say Hallel — because of the miracle.

lines.speaker: Objection
lines.text: Then why not Purim too? Its miracle is just as real!

lines.speaker: R' Yitzchak
lines.text: We do not sing Hallel for a miracle that occurred OUTSIDE the Land of Israel.

lines.speaker: Rav Naḥman b. Yitzchak objects
lines.text: But the Exodus was also a miracle outside the Land — and we say Hallel for it every Pesach!

lines.speaker: Resolution
lines.text: Before Israel entered the Land, every land was fit for song; entry gave the Land unique sanctity, excluding others — until exile restored their fitness. Rav Naḥman: reading the Megilla IS itself a form of Hallel. Rava: after the Exodus we could say 'servants of the LORD,' no longer Pharaoh's — but after Purim we remained subjects of Ahasuerus.

slides.title: 🔧 Temple Instruments — When 'Improvements' Made Things Worse
slides.subtitle: Craftsmanship anecdotes about the Temple's musical and ritual vessels

steps.content: 1️⃣ The Temple flute (reed, from the days of Moses) was gold-plated by royal command — its sweet sound was ruined; removing the plating restored it
2️⃣ The copper cymbal, damaged, was repaired by artisans from Alexandria — its sound worsened; undoing the repair restored it
3️⃣ The copper mortar used to grind incense spices suffered the same fate: an Alexandrian repair dulled its performance, and removing that repair brought it back

4️⃣ Both vessels survived from the FIRST Temple, damaged beyond true repair — echoing the Shiloach pool, widened to increase its flow but only diminished by it: 'let not the wise glory in his wisdom, nor the mighty in his might'

summary.principle: The Temple's precise ranges — trumpet blasts, instrument counts, and the specific days that carry full Hallel — reflect a system where every detail (how a sound is counted, what makes a day 'sanctified,' where a miracle occurred) is deliberately weighed, and where even a well-intentioned 'improvement' to a sacred vessel can undo what already worked.

flowSteps.content: 🎺 New mishna: trumpets (21–48), lyres (2–6), flutes (2–12); Rabbis count 3 separate blast-units, R' Yehuda counts 1
🎶 The flute's 12 days align with full-Hallel days: Sukkot daily (changing offerings), Pesach only day one, no Shabbat/Rosh Chodesh/RH/YK

columns.content: 🕎 Chanukah gets Hallel for its miracle; Purim does not — three different explanations offered
🔧 Gold-plating and outside repairs both ruined instruments the Sages had to restore by undoing the 'improvement'

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: precision — in counting sounds, defining sanctified days, and preserving original craftsmanship — governs even the Temple's music

quiz.q: According to the mishna, what is the minimum and maximum number of trumpet blasts sounded daily in the Temple?
o: A minimum of 7 and a maximum of 16
A minimum of 21 and a maximum of 48
A minimum of 2 and a maximum of 6
Always exactly 21, with no variation
quiz.e: The mishna sets the daily range at twenty-one blasts (for gate-opening and the two daily offerings) up to forty-eight on the Friday of Sukkot's water-drawing ceremony.

quiz.q: What is the essential disagreement between the Rabbis and Rabbi Yehuda over counting a series of shofar/trumpet blasts?
o: The Rabbis count tekiah, teruah, and tekiah as three separate units; Rabbi Yehuda counts the whole sequence as one unit
They disagree about which instrument should be used
The Rabbis require six blasts per day; Rabbi Yehuda requires none
They disagree about who is permitted to sound the blasts
quiz.e: This counting difference explains why the mishna's range (21–48) differs from Rabbi Yehuda's baraita (7–16) — the same physical sequence of sounds is simply tallied differently.

quiz.q: Why is the full Hallel recited every day of Sukkot but only on the first day of Pesach?
o: Because Sukkot's additional offerings differ from day to day, while Pesach's remain the same each day
Because Pesach is considered less important than Sukkot
Because Hallel may only be recited in the fall
Because Sukkot lasts longer, so more Hallel is required by default
quiz.e: The Gemara explains that each day of Sukkot has a distinct set of additional offerings (the bull count changes daily), making each day unique and Hallel-worthy, while Pesach's offerings are identical throughout.

quiz.q: According to Rabbi Abbahu, why is Hallel not recited on Rosh HaShana and Yom Kippur, even though both qualify as sanctified festivals?
o: Because these days fall in the autumn, when Hallel is never said
The ministering angels asked why Israel doesn't sing before God on these days, and He answered that joyous song is inappropriate while the King sits in judgment with the books of life and death open
Because no offerings are brought on those days
Because Rosh HaShana and Yom Kippur are not mentioned in the Torah
quiz.e: Rabbi Abbahu relates this exchange between the angels and God as the reason these solemn Days of Judgment lack the joyous recitation of Hallel.

quiz.q: What happened when the Temple's reed flute was plated with gold, according to the baraita?
o: Its sound became even more pleasant
Its pleasant sound was ruined; removing the gold plating restored the original sweet sound
It shattered and had to be replaced entirely
Nothing changed — the plating had no effect
quiz.e: The baraita reports that gold-plating the flute by royal command spoiled its sound, and only removing the plating brought back its original pleasant tone.
